newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - AUSTRALIAN JULY LABOUR FORCE DATA.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - AUSTRALIAN JULY LABOUR FORCE DATA.

text.p: Australian employment rose by 21,300 in July following a rise of 11,900 in June, The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Full-time employment rose by 52,500 in July.
The July unemployment rate was 8.7 percent, compared with 8.5 percent in June.
Forecasts for employment had centred on a 25,000 rise, and ranged from a rise of 12,000 to a rise of 50,000.
For, unemployment, forecasts centred on a rate of 8.6 percent and ranged from 8.3 to 8.8 percent.
A selection of economists' reactions to the data follows:
PETER MUNCKTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"The numbers were broadly in line with market expectations. It just continues to show that the labour market is in a very modest, almost flat, trend, which is not surprising when you look at business surveys and how the economy is growing."
RICHARD YETSENGA, ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"At face value it still shows the labour market is very subdued. The positive point is the strong rise in full-time employment in the month, which does at least a little bit to offset the big falls we have seen recently, though in trend terms it is still falling month-on-month. So it's still weak but perhaps a little more positive than it was."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"It was a very ordinary increase, except for the strong full time component. But even the strong full time component only takes it to 12,000 new full time jobs over three months, which is still not strong. We are encouraged by the number overall. But we were not expecting the drop off in part time employment. The RBA would look at this number and regard it as a reason to keep monetary policy on hold."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"To me the good news out of these figures is that full-time employment has picked up 52,500. Full-time employment has been extremely weak, so I think seeing a little bit of a pick-up in full-time is one big positive that I take out of today's figures. I wouldn't read too much into one month's employment figures though. They really do bounce around too much to read too much into them, but we should start seeing that flow-through of that first easing from July last year coming through. I think the recent, last month or two's, depreciation of the Australian dollar should also help in terms of adding a degree of stimulus to the economy."
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"The bounce back in full time is encouraging for the long term outlook for employment but there has been significant volatility in the relationship between full-time and part-time employment, so it may be a be too early to read too much into that number. The 8.7 percent unemployment rate confirms the pessimism we have seen among consusmers. It really focuses attention on the rate of economic growth in the economy. The unemployment rate is really stuck above 8.5 percent and we don't see that coming down in a hurry. The figures still maintain an easing bias to policy ... It certainly puts pressure on some policy response either from fiscal or monetary policy."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, JP MORGAN:
"We were expecting a sharp rise in full-time employment. The labour market is still subdued with the economy travelling at three percent. We are certainly not ruling out another rate cut."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:
"It was encouraging to see growth in full-time jobs. However, the overall pick-up in jobs was not enough to dent what remains an unacceptable rate of unemployment."

DAVID LANDSLEY, TREASURY ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK: "We think the labour market is moving sideways, there has been no improvement. The employment results are in line with with NAB's survey. We do not think today's figures encourage an optimistic view of another rate cut."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-9373-1800
